meta.title: Human-in-the-loop Agents
meta.thesis: Human-in-the-loop Agents is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A healthcare intake agent drafts answers but escalates risky medical and billing decisions to staff. By the end, they should be able to build or review human-review routing policy with approval and override paths, measure correct escalation rate, and catch the failure where the agent treats a judgment call as an automatic action.

mentalMap.title: Human-in-the-loop Agents: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Add human review where judgment, authority, or correction changes the outcome, then resume the agent with a recorded decision.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Human-in-the-loop agents work when the human sees a specific decision packet and the runtime can safely resume from it.

modules.title: Humans own judgment and authority
modules.sub: Use review for decisions the model should not own alone.
modules.summary: Human review should protect meaningful decisions.
objectives: Name reasons to put humans in the loop.

blocks.title: A human is not a decorative checkpoint

spans.text: Problem anchor: an agent drafts a public lesson from internal KB notes. The model can assemble a draft, but a human must approve copyright-sensitive citations and product claims before publication.

Humans are useful for authority, ambiguity, taste, policy exceptions, and high-impact side effects. They are not useful if the packet lacks evidence or if approval is required so often that reviewers stop reading.
If the reviewer cannot change the outcome, remove or redesign the checkpoint.

blocks.analogy: A good review gate is a decision desk, not a turnstile.

blocks.title: Case study: publish approval for lesson content

spans.text: The agent prepares a lesson, source list, known weak claims, and validation status. The reviewer can approve, request changes, or reject. The decision becomes part of the run state.
The human is not asked to inspect hidden reasoning. They inspect the artifact, evidence, and concrete risks.

items.text: Offer approve, edit/request changes, reject, or escalate.

blocks.title: Review purpose
blocks.prompt: Which decision is most appropriate for human review?

options.text: Counting tokens in a prompt.
Approving a customer-facing email that changes an account setting.
Parsing a JSON object with a schema validator.

blocks.explanation: Humans should guard judgment and authority, while deterministic checks handle mechanical validation.

modules.title: Choose interruption points deliberately
modules.sub: Interrupts should occur before irreversible or expensive actions.
modules.summary: The best interrupt is just before commitment.
objectives: Use interrupts for uncertainty and policy exceptions.

blocks.title: Timing determines whether review can help

spans.text: Interrupt too early and the human lacks context. Interrupt too late and the action is already done. The ideal point is after the agent gathers evidence and proposes a concrete action, before the external side effect.
LangGraph-style interrupts and durable workflow signals are useful because they persist state while waiting for human input and resume with the decision.
Every interrupt should have a timeout, owner, and safe default.

blocks.analogy: Review should happen while the door is unlocked, not after it has slammed shut.

cells.text: Approval before send, publish, delete, refund.
Action is external or hard to undo.
Model or evaluator detects missing evidence or ambiguity.

options.name: After completion only

cells.text: Actions are reversible or low risk.

options.whenToUse: Use as monitoring, not safety gate.

blocks.title: Interrupt placement
blocks.prompt: Where should review happen before publishing generated content?

options.text: After the content is already public.
After evidence and draft are ready, before the publish action runs.
Before the agent knows the topic.

blocks.explanation: Review needs enough context and must still be able to prevent the side effect.

modules.title: Present review packets, not raw traces
modules.sub: Humans need compact evidence and concrete choices.
modules.summary: The packet is the interface between agent and human.
objectives: Build a review packet with exact action details.
Avoid asking reviewers to infer hidden state.

blocks.title: A review packet should answer “what am I approving?”

spans.text: A useful packet includes the proposed action, arguments, artifact preview, supporting sources, policy reason for review, alternatives, and consequences of approve/edit/reject. It should hide irrelevant trace noise but link to full trace for audit.
The packet should not ask the human to approve hidden chain-of-thought. It should show observable evidence and concrete outputs.
A reviewer should be able to decide in under a minute for routine cases.

blocks.analogy: The review packet is an airport boarding pass: compact, specific, and linked to the full record.

blocks.title: Worked packet: approve a tool call

spans.text: For an email-send tool, the packet shows recipient, subject, body, source evidence, customer ID, risk tier, and the exact send button. It also offers edit, reject, and escalate.
If the body cites a policy, the cited source is included. If evidence is missing, the packet should recommend reject or request changes.

items.text: State the proposed action and exact arguments.
Show artifact preview and supporting evidence.
Offer explicit decision options and record rationale.

blocks.title: Packet design
blocks.prompt: What should be included in an approval packet for a database update?

options.text: Only “the model wants to update the database.”
The exact record, field changes, reason, evidence, risk, and approve/edit/reject options.
Only the model provider name.

blocks.explanation: Specific context lets humans exercise real authority.

modules.title: Resume safely after approval or correction
modules.sub: Human input becomes state, not a side conversation.
modules.summary: The agent should continue from the reviewed decision point.
objectives: Represent approve, edit, reject, and escalate.

blocks.title: The human decision is an event in the run

spans.text: After review, the runtime should resume with a structured decision: approved, rejected, edited arguments, requested changes, or escalation. The model may synthesize the next step, but application code applies the decision.
Spaced recall: from durable workflows, side effects before an interrupt must be idempotent or avoided. Otherwise resume can duplicate work.
Never ask the model to remember an approval from chat text alone; store it in run state.

blocks.title: Approval resume state machine
blocks.explanation: The decision changes structured state. Sending or publishing would happen only after the state reaches the approved branch.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict the status after the edit decision.
predictThenReveal.answer: The status becomes `needs_revision`, the draft is replaced, and the run is not approved.

blocks.title: Resume logic
blocks.prompt: Why store approval as structured state instead of only chat text?

options.text: Structured state prevents all model mistakes.
The runtime can deterministically branch, audit, and avoid repeating side effects.
Chat text cannot be displayed to humans.

blocks.explanation: Structured decisions make review enforceable by code.

modules.title: Measure review burden and missed escapes
modules.sub: HITL quality includes latency, load, and safety coverage.
objectives: Track approval latency and reviewer load.
Measure false positives and false negatives.

spans.text: Track how often the agent asks for review, how long reviewers take, how often they edit or reject, and which risky actions bypassed review. These numbers tell you whether the gate is useful or noisy.
Reviewers need escalation paths and sampled audits. High-severity cases may require two-person approval; low-risk repetitive cases may move to deterministic checks after evidence accumulates.
If reviewers approve 99% without edits, inspect whether the packet is too broad, too weak, or no longer needed.

blocks.title: Verify AI output after human review

spans.text: Use this checklist on runs that included a human decision.

items.text: The review packet showed exact action, artifact, evidence, and risk.
The decision was stored with reviewer, time, rationale, and any edits.
The resumed run followed the human decision rather than re-deciding it.
No irreversible side effect occurred before required approval.
Metrics track review latency, edit/reject rate, and missed-policy incidents.

blocks.title: Calibration signal
blocks.prompt: What does a high approval rate with no edits suggest?

options.text: The system no longer needs audit logs.
The review gate may be too broad, too low-value, or the packet may not reveal useful risks.
All future actions should skip policy checks.

blocks.explanation: Review gates should be calibrated with evidence, not assumed useful forever.

agent.label: Agent
agent.laymanDefinition: A software loop that plans, observes results, and may use tools to pursue a goal.
agent.technicalNote: Agent designs need explicit loop boundaries, stop conditions, permissions, state contracts, and evaluation surfaces before autonomy is useful.

tool.label: Tool
tool.laymanDefinition: An external capability the model can request, such as search, code execution, retrieval, or a business API.
tool.technicalNote: Tools require schemas, authorization, error handling, audit logs, and tests because natural-language intent is not execution permission.

state.label: State
state.laymanDefinition: The working information carried between steps of an agent workflow.
state.technicalNote: State should separate durable facts, transient scratch work, approvals, tool results, and failure metadata so retries and handoffs remain understandable.

memory.label: Memory
memory.laymanDefinition: Information saved across turns or sessions for future use.
memory.technicalNote: Agent memory needs scope, freshness, deletion, privacy controls, and evaluation so saved context helps rather than silently steering behavior.

mcp.label: MCP
mcp.laymanDefinition: A protocol for exposing tools and context to models and agent clients.
mcp.technicalNote: MCP-style integrations still need capability design, trust boundaries, lifecycle handling, and authorization around each exposed server.

sandbox.label: Sandbox
sandbox.laymanDefinition: An isolated environment that limits what agent actions can reach or change.
sandbox.technicalNote: Sandboxing should constrain files, network, processes, credentials, browser sessions, time, and side effects according to the task risk.

questions.q: Where does a human decision reduce risk or improve quality enough to justify interruption?
questions.why: Human review is costly; it should guard judgment, authority, and ambiguous evidence rather than rubber-stamp every step.
questions.rot: Interrupt at high-impact decisions with exact context, options, and recorded rationale.

questions.prompt: An agent is about to send a bulk email to 10,000 customers. At which point should a human approval interrupt be placed?

options.text: After the emails are sent, so the reviewer can see the real outcome
Before the send action executes, because sending is an irreversible side effect
Only if the agent's confidence score drops below 50%
Whenever the email list exceeds 1,000 recipients, but after drafting is complete

questions.explanation: Approval gates must sit before irreversible side effects — once the emails are sent, the action cannot be undone, so the interrupt must fire first.

questions.prompt: A reviewer is handed a raw agent execution trace — thousands of log lines — and asked to approve or reject the next action. What is the core problem with this approach?

options.text: Raw traces are too short to contain enough information for a decision
It forces the reviewer to infer hidden state rather than reading a prepared summary
Traces should only be shown after the action completes, not before
Reviewers should never see model outputs directly

questions.explanation: A review packet should surface the exact action, evidence, and model uncertainty in a readable form — asking reviewers to dig through raw traces shifts cognitive work onto them and increases error rates.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes 'review theater'?

options.text: A structured process where reviewers watch a live demo of the agent before approving it for production
Routing every agent action through a human regardless of risk, creating the appearance of oversight without real judgment
A dashboard that visualizes reviewer approval latency over time
Escalating low-confidence decisions to a senior reviewer instead of the primary one

questions.explanation: Review theater happens when human review is performed as a ritual rather than a genuine check — volume is so high or context so thin that reviewers rubber-stamp decisions, providing no real safety benefit.

questions.prompt: After a reviewer edits an agent's proposed action before approving it, what must the system do before resuming execution?

options.text: Restart the entire agent run from the beginning to ensure consistency
Persist the reviewer's edited decision and predict the downstream state that will result from the corrected action
Log the original action and proceed with it anyway to avoid branching logic
Escalate automatically, because any edit signals the agent is unreliable

questions.explanation: Safe resumption requires storing the reviewer's decision durably and reasoning about what world-state the corrected action will produce — skipping this step risks the agent continuing with stale or inconsistent assumptions.

questions.prompt: Name one metric that reveals reviewers are overburdened AND one metric that reveals the human-in-the-loop system is missing real problems. Briefly explain what each metric measures.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Overburdened: approval latency (time reviewers take to respond, which rises when queue depth exceeds capacity) or reviewer load (number of reviews per person per unit time). Missing real problems: false negative rate (the share of harmful or incorrect agent actions that passed through review without being caught), which can be tracked by feeding post-incident analysis back into the trigger system.
questions.explanation: Approval latency and reviewer load expose bottlenecks on the human side; false negatives (missed escapes) expose gaps in what the system routes for review — both dimensions must be monitored to keep the loop healthy.
